newsitem.title: USA: Cars, home-improvement, sales top consumer frauds.
newsitem.headline: Cars, home-improvement, sales top consumer frauds.

text.p: Consumer advocates said on Tuesday that car repairs and sales, home-improvement and marketing remain top areas for consumer fraud.
Complaints over confusing car leases were rising, as was fraud targetted at Spanish-speaking consumers. And a new area for bilking consumers may be in the retailing of natural gas and electricity.

"Consumers continue to lose billions of dollars each year to deception and fraud," said Joseph Goldberg, president of the National Association of Consumer Agency Administrators, a group of state and local government consumer offices.
Next year, there could be increased complaints as federal deregulation allows retailers to buy gas and electricity from public utilities for reasale to homeowners.
Goldberg said these fraudulent retailers may take a home-owner's payment for future delivery of gas or electricity but then pocket the money and not deliver the service.
He also said complaints may rise from Internet commerce, as telemarketing fraud migrates to the increasingly popular computer network.

"Stronger consumer protections and more aggressive consumer education are needed to address these problems adequately," said Goldberg, who is director of the Bureau of Consumer Protection in the Pennsylvania Attorney General's office.

Stephen Brobeck, executive director of the Consumer Federation of America, comprised of 240 non-profit advocacy groups, said the worst fraud was committed by small companies, but added that big firms were not immune.
Car leasing has become the focus of growing complaints because consumers "did not understand the contract they signed," the groups said in a statement.
"Many believed that they were purchasing, not leasing, the car," they said, while others complained about the substantial lease termination penalties and excess wear-and-tear charges.

Mary Ponder, the federation's director of special projects, said that the car leasing industry favored complex contracts because it makes if difficult for consumers to compare prices and find the best deal. But she said that new federal disclosure regulations that take effect next October would correct some of these problems.
Ponder said that state attorneys generals and the Federal Trade Commission were negotiating with the industry to try to end questionable leasing practices, but gave no details.
An FTC spokeswoman said the agency had no comment on any specific actions it might take, but "car leasing has been a concern of ours" and that it had acted in past cases.
The groups said there were many complaints last year from Spanish-speaking consumers.
They cited cases where Spanish-speakers negotiated a car lease in Spanish but then were asked to sign contracts in English that did not reflect their verbal agreements.
"They can be can be easy prey solely because of the language difficulty," Goldberg said.

The groups said that other major fraud areas last year included furniture sales, credit repair, landlord-tenant dealings, appliance repairs, immigration dealings, health spa memberships, modeling contracts and work-at-home schemes.
